title: When Does the Market Matter? Stock Prices and the Investment of Equity-Dependent Firms
research_question: Does the link between corporate investment and stock prices differ depending on whether firms need external equity to finance their marginal investments? Specifically, do firms reliant on outside equity exhibit a stronger response of investment to nonfundamental movements in their share prices, and do their equity issuance patterns similarly track stock-price valuations?
data_description: The study uses an unbalanced annual panel of Compustat firms covering 1980 through 1999, excluding financial firms (one-digit SIC of six) and firm-years with book value under $10 million, yielding 52,101 firm-year observations (about 2,605 per year). Stock return data come from CRSP. Key variables include four investment measures (capital expenditures, capex plus R&D, capex plus R&D plus SG&A, and growth in book assets, all scaled by lagged assets), external equity issues and total external finance (equity plus debt) scaled by lagged assets, Tobin's Q (market value of equity plus assets minus book equity, over assets), operating cash flow over assets, three-year cumulative future stock returns, and a Kaplan-Zingales-based index of equity dependence built from cash flow, dividends, cash balances, and leverage, supplemented by firm age (years since IPO) and industry cash-flow volatility.
institutional_context: The setting is U.S. publicly listed nonfinancial corporations during the 1980s and 1990s, a period featuring substantial variation in stock-market valuations and equity-issuance activity. The institutional motivation is the long-running debate about whether stock prices influence real corporate investment because they reflect fundamentals (the marginal product of capital, à la Tobin's Q) or because nonfundamental price movements alter the effective cost of external equity, as suggested by Keynes and later developed by Bosworth, Fischer-Merton, Morck-Shleifer-Vishny, Blanchard-Rhee-Summers, and Stein. Standard corporate-finance frictions—adverse selection in seasoned equity offerings, leverage constraints, limited debt capacity for young firms with volatile cash flows, and reliance on retained earnings versus outside finance—create heterogeneity across firms in how dependent they are on issuing equity to fund marginal projects, generating a setting where mispricing can plausibly translate into real investment distortions for some firms but not others.
ground_truth_notes: The exact sample period is not specified, and the reliance on the KZ index as a proxy may introduce some measurement error.
